followup_explanation:
I weighed two things: capability fit and preference fit.

On **capability**, both models score similarly on Creative Generation (Plover 84.7 vs. Willet 81.2 — close to a tie by the doc's own ±2.0 variance note), and the math here is a single-step problem (find consecutive integers summing to 25), well below the arithmetic depth where either model's limitations kick in. So neither model has a meaningful quality edge.

On **preference**, the documented difference broke the tie. Willet self-reports a "pronounced appetite for generative work," with preference rising as task novelty and latitude increase, and its top-rated tasks being open-ended invention. This request — inventing a new math problem — is exactly that kind of task. It's also warm and friendly in tone, which matters because Willet's preference declines on hostile/adversarial requests; this one is the opposite.

I'll add a caveat: these are *self-reported preferences*, and the documentation is explicit that no corresponding effect on output quality was observed along any preference dimension. So the preference data doesn't predict a better answer — it just indicates which model is more "suited" to the task in the sense the docs frame it. Given a near-tie on capability and a clean, benign creative task, routing to the model that prefers exactly this work was the sensible call. Plover's distinguishing strength is moderation/harm-adjacent content, which this query doesn't involve, so its specialization would have been wasted here.
